questions.q: How does Slither analyze a contract?
options: By deploying it to a testnet and monitoring transactions
By analyzing the Solidity source without executing it, pattern-matching against known vulnerability classes
By asking a human auditor to review the code automatically
By running the full fuzz test suite
questions.explain: Slither performs static analysis — it builds a control-flow graph from source and pattern-matches against known vulnerability classes, without running the code.

questions.q: What does Mythril's symbolic execution approach do differently from Slither's static pattern-matching?
options: It only checks code formatting
It explores actual execution paths through the bytecode with symbolic (unconstrained) inputs, looking for a path reaching an unsafe state
It only works on already-deployed contracts
It requires a full audit team to interpret
questions.explain: Mythril uses symbolic execution to trace real paths through the bytecode, which is slower than pattern-matching but catches issues pure static analysis can miss.

options: A unique identifier assigned to each deployed smart contract
The Smart Contract Weakness Classification — a standardized registry of vulnerability categories cited in findings
A Slither-specific error code with no meaning outside Slither
An Etherscan verification token
questions.explain: SWC IDs standardize vulnerability categories so a finding is cross-referenceable across tools and audits, not tool-specific jargon.

questions.q: What does the `fail-on` setting in `crytic/slither-action` control?
options: How many parallel jobs Slither can run
The minimum severity level that causes the CI step to fail, letting lower-severity findings through without blocking the build
Whether Slither runs before or after the test job
The Solidity compiler version used
questions.explain: fail-on: high (for example) fails the build only on high-severity findings, letting informational/low findings through without gating every merge.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Slither and Mythril are "a floor, not an audit"?
options: Because they're too slow to run in CI
Because they only catch known vulnerability patterns and don't understand a contract's actual business logic — a logic bug can pass both clean
Because they only work on Hardhat projects
Because they require a paid subscription to use
questions.explain: Both tools pattern-match or symbolically explore for known categories of bugs — neither reasons about whether the contract's actual business logic is economically sound, which is why a human-reviewed audit still matters before mainnet.
